title: Silo
creator: Hugh Howey, Graham Yost, Aric Avelino, Jessica Kaplan, Jeffery Wang, Cassie Pappas, Ingrid Escajeda
review:
I’d give the first season of Silo a 7 out of 10. It’s pretty alright, and the acting is genuinely good, but beyond that, I don't have many praises to offer. The story so far doesn’t really interest me because it feels like a very basic human containment dystopia. Nothing about the show stands out or does anything unique with its premise. In fact, the silo itself is ultimately just set dressing; you could replace it with almost any other isolated environment and the core story wouldn't change at all.
It’s a trope we've seen countless times in media, and I think a lot of other properties have done it much better. When you look at compelling human containment systems in stories like The Giver, Attack on Titan, The Maze Runner, The Hunger Games, The 100, The Matrix, or Snowpiercer, Silo feels incredibly derivative. It’s essentially structured exactly like Snowpiercer, except it’s a vertical bunker instead of a sideways train.
Where the show really loses me is in the lazy writing surrounding its worldbuilding. There are only 10,000 humans left in this bunker, yet they still operate under a capitalist system using a fabricated currency called "credits." It feels unnecessary. In a closed survival system of that size, societal pressures and the basic human need for self-fulfillment would be more than enough to make people work for the good of the silo. Furthermore, for a dystopia, there is surprisingly little oppression. There doesn't seem to be any systemic malice in the structure itself. Even the people at the very bottom levels are treated well and aren't starving. Everyone is provided for, so it just feels like nothing bad is actually happening. What is the point of the story, then?
This lack of organic conflict spills over into the characters and how the show handles its villains. Robert Sims initially seems like the primary threat, playing the basic trope of the poor janitor's son who clawed his way up to do Judicial's dirty work, like throwing people off ladders. However, it turns out he just works for the current mayor, Bernard Holland, who is the true final antagonist of the season. But even Bernard doesn't come across as a malicious villain. If you look at it from his point of view, his actions make sense based on what he genuinely believes is good for the silo. He is simply way too pragmatic, viewing human sacrifices as a necessary evil for survival rather than acting out of intentional cruelty. With the main antagonist acting out of cold pragmatism instead of malice, and others in power (like the judge and the previous mayor) appearing completely clueless or genuinely kind, the central conflict feels flat.
Finally, as a mystery, Silo stumbles badly. A good mystery is like a puzzle: you need to have the pieces to be able to figure it out. If you don't have the pieces but are still expected to solve it, or if everything is hidden until a massive exposition dump in the final episodes, it isn't a good puzzle. You aren't thinking; you are just a passive observer. And when the show does drop clues, they are far too obvious. When the former sheriff told Jules to "double the flowers in front of the mirror," it wasn't some grand brain teaser. It immediately gave away that the mirrors hide cameras in a surveillance state.
Fans of the show might promise that "massive twists are coming" in the final episodes, but if you can see them coming a mile away, they aren't really twists. Even if the finale turns everything on its head, being unpredictable at the very last second isn't the same as earning a reveal. Ultimately, Silo is an okay watch, but it simply isn't smart enough to compare with Severance, per example, even though that isn't a fair comparison.

title: Bridgerton
creator: Chris Van Dusen, Julia Quinn
review:
Season 1 of Bridgerton was certainly a pleasure to watch. While period dramas and romance fall outside of my usual interests, the gossip and drama of 1813 London's high society are more than enough to keep me hooked throughout. Although the central love stories don't personally draw me in as much, I can definitely appreciate how essential they are to driving the show's overall plot and tension.

Lady Agatha Danbury, portrayed brilliantly by Adjoa Andoh, quickly became my favorite character of the season. Her quick and accurate judgment of everyone in a room, along with her disregard for the rigid rules of high society, made me wish I was half as sharp as her. Her deep connection to the late Duchess of Hastings and her role as a mentor to Simon, the current Duke, drew me to her character even further.

Across the board, the acting is strong, particularly in how the cast navigates the gray morality of their characters. Everyone feels complex rather than cartoonishly evil in their portrayals. Even Queen Charlotte shows surprising depth, despite her cold remarks about waiting for the King to pass, you can see moments of genuine love and heartbreak for the man he used to be.

The reveal of Lady Whistledown's true identity felt a bit obvious, especially after Penelope's falling out with Marina over Colin. However, despite Whistledown's identity becoming known to the viewer, it doesn't diminish the value of her commentary or the chaos her writing unleashes over each episode.

Overall, Bridgerton delivers a stylish, dramatic, and surprisingly addictive first season. It balances gray, nuanced characters and sharp social commentary well enough that even non romance fans can find plenty to enjoy.

title: Good Omens
creator: Neil Gaiman, Terry Pratchett
review:
Season 1 of Good Omens was an absolute joy to watch, Terry Pratchett's writing is just so inspired and full of tiny joys. While Neil Gaiman brings the grit and slight dread of living in a universe where all the decisions have already been made for you.

Season 2 was also a joy to watch, the story felt slightly disjointed but i still rather enjoyed it. I would never have expected Gabriel to Fall in love with Beelzebub.
Did the story feel good? Not particularly. But I adore watching Aziraphale, played by Michael Sheen, and Crowley, played by David Tennant, interact with each other.
The betrayal and rejection of Crowley at the end made me miserable for days and I couldn't wait for the third and final season to come out.

but..

Neil Gaiman just couldn't keep it in his pants.

After two years the allegations were dropped and charges were cleared but the damage was already done and the show had been canceled.
The actors and the rest of the team worked hard and were able to convince Amazon to allow them to produce a 90 minute movie in place of the six episodes the season was supposed to have.

Then on May 13, 2026, the movie released.

I anxiously watched it in-between university classes with my boyfriend over discord.
It was a great experience and the movie itself wasn't as bad as I originally expected it to be.
It was not a great movie by any stretch of the word, but I can appreciate it for what it is.
The story was rushed, the ending was controversial, a lot changed since season 1.
But I got closure for these characters that I hold so dear to my heart.

Aziraphale: the lazy gluttonous angel that just couldn't keep himself from having this higher than thou attitude towards everyone else.
Crowley: the good intentioned demon that didn't so much Fall as saunter vaguely downwards.
They both mean so much to me and i will forever keep them close to my religiously traumatized heart.

Through all the high highs and all the low lows, I love this show and highly recommend it to all who are willing to give it a try.

title: Daemons of the Shadow Realm
creator: Hiromu Arakawa
review: Hiromu Arakawa is an excellent writer. Her use of duality throughout the story has already made me reflect on the dualities within myself. Chaos and order, strength and vulnerability. I am looking forward to seeing where she takes this story.
